prompt: A project's CONTRIBUTING.md says new feature requests must first be discussed on a community forum before any GitHub issue is opened. An issue titled 'Add per-model configurable caching' was opened directly on GitHub with no prior forum discussion. What does this tell you about that issue, even if it's labeled 'good first issue'?
choices: Nothing — labels always override the general CONTRIBUTING.md process
It was filed against the project's own stated process, which is itself a red flag for whether it's actually ready to be worked on
It means the issue is higher priority than normal bug reports
It means the maintainers have already approved the feature design

prompt: A repo's CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md file is only three lines long and just links to an external page on the organization's website. What's the correct read of this?
choices: The project doesn't really enforce a code of conduct
This is a common pattern on large projects — the real policy lives on an org-wide page so it can be updated once instead of per-repo, and it still functions as an enforced floor on behavior
The file is broken and should be reported as a bug
Code of conduct files are purely decorative and can be ignored either way

prompt: An issue template's config.yml contains `blank_issues_enabled: false`. What does this actually do?
choices: It closes all currently open issues automatically
It removes the option to open a freeform/blank issue, forcing every new issue through one of the defined templates
It prevents maintainers from commenting on issues
It disables issue creation entirely until a maintainer re-enables it

prompt: In the fork -> branch -> PR workflow, what is the correct purpose of adding a remote named `upstream`?
choices: `upstream` is where you push your own branches for review
`upstream` points at the original project so you can fetch its latest `main` and branch from it, while `origin` stays your own fork that you push to
`upstream` and `origin` are two names for the exact same remote and either can be used interchangeably
`upstream` is only needed after your PR has already been merged

prompt: A reviewer asks for a change on your open pull request. What's the correct way to respond in git, and why?
choices: Force-push a rewritten, amended commit over the one they reviewed, since it keeps history clean
Close the PR and open a brand new one with the fix included from the start
Add a new commit addressing the feedback and push it normally — this keeps the reviewer's existing comments attached to the code they were made on, instead of orphaning them
Ask the reviewer to make the change themselves since they found the issue

prompt: Which single signal is the strongest warning sign that a 'good first issue'-labeled issue is actually a trap?
choices: The issue has a clear, specific file and line referenced
A maintainer commented within the last month confirming it's still valid
The issue has had no activity in over a year, or 15+ comments with unresolved disagreement about what the fix should even be
The issue is unassigned with no linked pull request

prompt: A maintainer leaves a blunt review comment pointing out a missing regression test and an undocumented breaking change, with no softening language. What is the professional, non-defensive response?
choices: Argue that the original code also had this problem, so it isn't really your fault
Go silent for a couple of weeks until the discomfort passes
Address each concrete point directly: add the test, document the breaking change, and say so clearly, citing what was actually changed
Close the pull request rather than deal with the feedback

prompt: After a maintainer merges your pull request (commonly via squash merge), what should you do with your fork and local branch before starting new work?
choices: Leave everything as-is indefinitely; it has no effect on future contributions
Delete your entire fork and re-fork the project from scratch
Pull the real project's updated main into your fork's main, push that to origin, and delete the now-merged feature branch both locally and on your fork
Force-push your feature branch's history onto the upstream project's main branch
